content.title: Why UConn women struggled in Final Four vs. South Carolina
content.text: PHOENIX, ARIZONA - APRIL 3: Raven Johnson #25 and Ta'niya Latson #00 of the South Carolina Gamecocks react after winning a NCAA Women's Final Four semifinal game against the UConn Huskies at Mortgage Matchup Center on April 3, 2026 in Phoenix, Arizona. (Photo by Ben Solomon/NCAA Photos via Getty Images)Ben Solomon/NCAA Photos via Getty ImagesFrom 2020 through 2024, South Carolina dominated its series with the UConn women's basketball team winning five out of six meetings.Led by center Aliyah Boston, the Gamecocks' athleticism, size and defense were too much for the Huskies to handle. Only once did UConn score more than 65 points and that was in a four-point loss in Hartford in 2023. Three times it was held under 60 -- including a 64-49 loss in the 2022 national championship game in Minneapolis.Article continues below this adGet Digital Access and Stay Informed With Trusted Local News.Get Digital Access and Stay Informed With Trusted Local News.ONLY 25¢But a year ago, the Huskies stayed healthy and gave Paige Bueckers the help she needed as they routed the Gamecocks in the regular season and in the final in Tampa, Fla., breaking 80 points in both games.With Bueckers watching from the Mortgage Matchup Center stands Friday in Phoenix, the national semifinal between UConn and South Carolina looked like 2022. With the Huskies' best players struggling, the Gamecocks ended UConn's reign as national champion and its 54-game winning streak, pulling away for a convincing 62-48 victory.Only once in their 171-game NCAA Tournament history have the Huskies scored fewer points. That came in a 1992 second-round loss in Nashville when they fell to Vanderbilt 75-47, which is also their worst loss in their NCAA Tournament history.Article continues below this adUConn was held to 31.1 percent shooting from the floor (19 for 61) and 28.6 percent from 3-point land (6 for 21). It also got the foul line only six times.Its "Big Three" of national Player of the Year Sarah Strong (12), All-American Azzi Fudd (8) and freshman Blanca Quiñonez (7) combined for only 27 points. The Huskies started well enough, scoring 13 points in the opening six minutes but then struggled after the media time out when coach Geno Auriemma went to his bench to put in his reliable top substitutes -- Quiñonez and Kayleigh Heckel. UConn scored only 13 points the rest of the half though it was enough to take a 26-24 edge to the locker room.Article continues below this adSouth Carolina opened the second half with a 16-4 run to go up by 10. The Huskies' 3-point then came alive as Heckel, Quiñonez and Fudd hit treys in a one-minute span to cut the gap to one.They were still within 46-44 with 6:37 left before the Gamecocks closed with a second 16-4 run to take it going away.Strong was only 4-for-16 from the floor, some misses from being well-guarded by SEC Defensive Player of the Year Raven Johnson and some misses of shots she's made consistently for her two college seasons. It was the third time this season the sophomore failed to hit at least half of her shots.Fudd was 3-for-15 from the floor and one of the most prolific 3-pointers shooters in UConn history was only 2-for-9 from behind the arc. Tessa Johnson gets credit for South Carolina, but the confidence the graduate student guard showed in winning Final Four Most Outstanding Player honors a year ago was not there as she passed up opportunities when she appeared open.Article continues below this adQuiñonez was 2-for-6 shooting and was in foul trouble. But relying on a freshman in the Final Four is not usually the winning edge.And it wasn't Friday.South Carolina also controlled the boards 47-32 with All-American Joyce Edwards making it tough for UConn in the lane.Article continues below this adThe result was the Huskies' fifth loss in six games when playing the opener of the national semifinal doubleheader. Overall, they are 13-12 in national semifinals.UConn finishes 38-1.Get daily updates from the UConn basketball world.April 3, 2026|Updated April 3, 2026 11:27 p.m.Carl Adamec has covered the UConn women's basketball team for close to 40 years, dating back to the early days of the Geno Auriemma era. A graduate of Putnam High in Connecticut and St. John's University in New York, he's been honored by the Connecticut Girls Soccer Coaches Association and Connecticut American Legion baseball program in his time at the JI and was inducted into the United States Basketball Writers Association Hall of Fame as part of the Class of 2023.
